The classical clutter filtering problem is thus to recover v v by suppressing s s . However, posing this problem as such may be an oversimplification of the reality: in practice, tissue and flow signals can exhibit overlapping spatiotemporal dynamics, making removal of unwanted clutter non-trivial. Nonetheless, a robust method to tackle this problem is to exploit the spatiotemporal correlations of the data. This can be performed by reshaping the ultrasound data into a Casorati matrix formulation, where the spatial (pixel) dimensions p = ( x , z ) p=(x,z) are vectorized into a single index of length N p = N x × N z N_{p}=N_{x}\times N_{z} : 𝐔 ∈ ℂ N p × N t \mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{C}^{N_{p}\times N_{t}} (2) 𝐔 = [ u ⁡ ( p 1 , t 1 ) u ⁡ ( p 1 , t 2 ) ⋯ u ⁡ ( p 1 , t N t ) u ⁡ ( p 2 , t 1 ) u ⁡ ( p 2 , t 2 ) ⋯ u ⁡ ( p 2 , t N t ) ⋱ u ⁡ ( p N p , t 1 ) u ⁡ ( p N p , t 2 ) ⋯ u ⁡ ( p N p , t N t ) ] \mathbf{U}=\begin{bmatrix}u(p_{1},t_{1})&u(p_{1},t_{2})&\cdots&u(p_{1},t_{N_{t}})\\ u(p_{2},t_{1})&u(p_{2},t_{2})&\cdots&u(p_{2},t_{N_{t}})\\ \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\ u(p_{N_{p}},t_{1})&u(p_{N_{p}},t_{2})&\cdots&u(p_{N_{p}},t_{N_{t}})\end{bmatrix} (3) where each column 𝐔 ( : , t k ) \mathbf{U}(:,t_{k}) represents a full spatial frame at observed time t k t_{k} , and each row 𝐔 ( p i , : ) \mathbf{U}(p_{i},:) is the temporal signal at pixel p i p_{i} .

Clutter filtering can be performed directly on 𝐔 \mathbf{U} ; however, a more principled approach is to operate on the second-order statistics, i.e., the covariance matrix. Often this will be the temporal covariance matrix since it is more computationally- and memory-efficient. III-A Ultrasound Data Ultrasound ensembles were acquired in n = 10 n=10 wild-type C57BL6 mice (male, 6–8 weeks old) under ketamine/xylazine sedation with continuous Sonovue microbubble infusion (15 μ \mu L/min). All animal procedures and husbandry were carried out in accordance with the recommendations of the Canadian Council on Animal Care (CCAC) and have been approved by the local McGill University Animal Care Committee. IQ data at 50% bandwidth sampling were recorded on a Verasonics Vantage & NXT scanner with gapless acquisition, using int16 and half datatypes across datasets. Beamformed images were coherently compounded from 11 tilted plane waves ( − 5 ∘ -5^{\circ} to 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} ) at a PRF of 1000 Hz, acquired at 15.6 MHz with a 128-element linear array (L22-14v, Vermon). Sessions lasted 30–40 minutes, yielding ∼ \sim 2 TB per session. Images were beamformed via GPU-accelerated delay-and-sum (DAS).

AER was implemented with the ZCA weighting: the SVD of the regularized covariance yielded eigenvectors U U and eigenvalues Λ \Lambda used to construct the whitening matrix W W . For the temporal case, we first arrange the data into the Casorati formulation, with space along one dimension and time along the other, then construct the temporal covariance matrix by transposition and multiplication.

The whitening matrix is obtained by taking the SVD of this covariance matrix and rescaling its eigenvalues accordingly, achieving temporal whitening. Because data were acquired gaplessly, an arbitrary number of temporal samples can be incorporated; doing so, however, grows the size of the covariance matrix and increases computational complexity. III-B 2 AER of the Spatial Covariance Spatial AER follows a similar procedure to temporal AER, but operates on the spatial covariance matrix instead. Because the spatial dimensions do not grow with time, computational complexity remains more manageable than for temporal operations, given that the number of spatial samples stays fixed. Here, the spatial covariance was constructed iteratively by accumulating outer products of spatial vectors from each time frame, then normalizing by the number of frames, as shown in Algorithm III-B2 . This running accumulation lets the spatial covariance be estimated from arbitrarily long temporal ensembles without holding every frame in memory at once.

For the whole-brain temporal covariance comparisons, tracking was performed using the complete tracking-prior-to-localization workflow of Leconte et al. [ 4 ] , applied identically to SVD- and ZCA-filtered data. For the long-ensemble spatial covariance comparisons, this full workflow was not used, as its centerline-thinning step failed to form complete capillary tracks on these data. Instead, only the Hessian-based vesselness filter from [ 4 ] was retained to generate an approximate a priori confidence map of bubble location from the lag-1 correlation image. Candidate bubble positions were localized as local maxima of the radial-symmetry response within this map, and candidates were linked across frames using the Hungarian algorithm [ 22 ] . This reduced pipeline compensated for frame gaps and recovered additional stationary bubbles that were otherwise discarded by the full workflow.

III-D Parameter Optimization The regularization parameter λ \lambda was swept from 1 to 1000 to characterize clutter, flow, and noise power tradeoffs (Section IV ), and from 1 to 80 for capillary-count optimization on the subcortical ROI. For each value of λ \lambda , clutter, flow, and noise power were estimated by taking the temporal Fourier transform of the filtered signal at each pixel, spanning the full, unfolded 0–1000 Hz range set by the 1000 Hz PRF (IQ data have no Nyquist fold), and computing the mean power within a corresponding frequency band: clutter as 0–1 Hz, flow as 1–500 Hz, and noise as > > 500 Hz. The clutter cutoff (1 Hz) was set empirically as the lowest boundary that isolated stationary tissue without including slow flow (a 5 Hz cutoff was also tested but included visibly moving structures); the noise cutoff (500 Hz) was set at half the frame rate. The same band definitions were used for the capillary-count optimization sweep. Temporal ensemble size for the spatial-covariance analysis was optimized by measuring the effective rank of the eigenvalue spectrum of the spatial covariance matrix, defined as the participation ratio R = ( ∑ k λ k ) 2 ∑ k λ k 2 . R=\frac{\left(\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\right)^{2}}{\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}^{2}}. (16) This measure quantifies the effective number of eigenmodes contributing comparable variance to the spectrum, i.e., how concentrated or spread the eigenvalue distribution is, rather than a literal count of independent flow components. An ensemble length of 15 s was selected from the plateau in R R as a function of ensemble size and used for all subsequent spatial AER comparisons.

III-E Single Capillary Reporters (SCaRe) Capillary-level flow recovery was quantified using the Single Capillary Reporter (SCaRe) framework [ 8 ] , which uses a hidden Markov model (HMM) trained on bubble trajectories to identify a characteristic U-shaped velocity profile: a transition from high-velocity arteriolar inflow, through a low-velocity capillary transit, to high-velocity venous outflow. Dwell time is defined as the duration the HMM assigns to the low-velocity capillary state, and a trajectory is counted as a complete capillary track when the full arteriole-capillary-venule sequence is recovered. IV Results IV-A AER balances high spatiotemporal coherent signals to noise Because SVD filtering reconstructs the temporal stack as a linear combination of a subset of eigenspaces, the SVD-filtered result may still retain conventional speckle noise, whereas in the whitened data, where the tissue subspace has been suppressed by rescaling its eigenvalues to the noise floor, the residual noise and tissue signal is white (see Supplementary Video 1). This is also reflected in the covariance domain (Fig. 1 , bottom): after SVD filtering, in which the large eigenvalues corresponding to highly coherent tissue signal are removed, the covariance retains a strong diagonal but exhibits residual off-diagonal spatiotemporal correlations, whereas the covariance of the whitened dataset closely approximates the identity, as expected from Equation 11 , indicating that each spatiotemporal index is uncorrelated. This decorrelation is directly reflected in the single-frame image quality shown in Fig. 1 (top). To build intuition for how AER reshapes the signal at the pixel level, we plot the in-phase (I) against the quadrature (Q) component over time at three representative points (Fig.

2 ): a stationary, temporally coherent signal, such as skull or tissue, traces an elongated, off-center scatter, since successive I and Q samples are correlated, while a fully decorrelated signal produces a circular cloud centered at zero. At the skull (first row), SVD filtering partially recenters the distribution but leaves a directional, correlated structure, whereas ZCA removes it entirely. The same pattern holds at a large cortical vessel (second row); at a large artery near the base of the brain (third row), SVD and ZCA perform similarly, likely because the signal there already approximates a decorrelated distribution before filtering. This decorrelation is particularly beneficial for slow microbubble flow, which shares clutter’s temporal coherence and is therefore easily discarded by rank-based filters like SVD; because AER rescales rather than discards eigenmodes, these weak, slow-moving signals are more likely to be preserved. As described in Equation 14 , the ZCA weighting includes a regularization parameter λ \lambda to stabilize the matrix inversion, introducing a free parameter that may influence clutter suppression performance: setting λ = λ 1 \lambda=\lambda_{1} yields no filtering, whereas setting λ = λ n \lambda=\lambda_{n} whitens all eigenspaces to the noise floor of the dataset, and varying λ \lambda modulates the texture of the output from speckle noise toward white noise. We therefore characterized the reconstructed dataset as a function of λ \lambda , sweeping it from 1 to 1000 (corresponding to 1 second of data at 1000 fps) for a single RF buffer and estimating clutter, flow, and noise power as described in Section III-D ; in the SVD case, λ \lambda plays the equivalent role of the eigenvalue cutoff used for flow reconstruction. Fig. 3 (top) shows the resulting normalized power for ZCA (solid lines) and SVD (dotted lines). According to Fig. 3 , the clutter signal drops off immediately in both cases, though more gradually for ZCA, while flow and noise both increase with λ \lambda ; noise eventually overtakes flow, but this crossover occurs later for ZCA than for SVD. The largest difference, however, is that flow is recovered across the entire eigenvalue spectrum for ZCA, whereas it is heavily attenuated in SVD outside a narrow range. Fig.

3 (bottom) shows representative reconstructions for each Fourier band at λ = 1 \lambda=1 , 26 26 , and 1000 1000 to visualize the performance of the clutter filtering across all λ \lambda values. This qualitative comparison illustrates the same divergence directly. At λ = 1 \lambda=1 , SVD and ZCA are visually indistinguishable across all three bands, consistent with λ = λ 1 \lambda=\lambda_{1} corresponding to no filtering. At λ = 26 \lambda=26 , near the peak of the flow curves, both methods recover a well-defined vascular pattern in the flow band with comparably suppressed clutter. At λ = 1000 \lambda=1000 , however, the two methods diverge sharply: for SVD, the clutter band has collapsed to a flat, saturated value with no discernible structure and the flow band has been reduced to unstructured noise, while for ZCA a faint clutter pattern remains visible and, more notably, the vascular flow pattern is still clearly resolved despite the added noise texture. This confirms qualitatively that flow information collapses under heavy SVD regularization while it is preserved, at the cost of added noise, under heavy ZCA whitening. In AER terms (Equation 9 ), increasing λ \lambda gives every flow mode past the SVD cutoff zero weight, whereas ZCA only lowers the rescaling floor, so all flow modes keep a nonzero weight. In practice, this indicates that ZCA is more forgiving to the choice of regularizer than SVD: a single λ \lambda can be reused across acquisitions that differ in microbubble concentration, imaging depth, or skull thickness, without re-tuning for each dataset, and flow reconstruction remains stable even as clutter and noise levels drift over a long acquisition. IV-C ZCA increases the number of trajectories We can view the effects of ZCA on the temporal covariance in the tracking behavior on the same dataset across low and high concentration regimes (Fig. 4 ). In low concentration, ZCA recovers more trajectories across the whole field of view, indicating that attenuation is inherently compensated, and tracking artifacts concentrated at the skull-brain interface under SVD are visibly reduced. The same trend holds, and is further enhanced, at high concentration: for the same amount of data, ZCA recovers more trajectories, suggesting that comparable ULM maps could be constructed with less data. This difference is most apparent in the central and peripheral vascular arcs of Fig. 4 : under SVD, only fragments of the arborizing network are recovered, with visible gaps between disconnected trajectory segments, whereas under ZCA the same field of view shows a near-continuous, fully arborized network. The improvement is most pronounced in the high-concentration case, where SVD still leaves gaps at the periphery that ZCA fills in almost completely. This increase in trajectory density is directly visible in the resulting cortical vasculature (Fig. 5 ). On large vessels like the vein, both methods yield the same vascular profile, indicating full reconstruction, but the ZCA profile line shows greater definition in smaller penetrating arterioles, along with new vasculature separable from noise and a shift in the estimated vessel center. This is consistent with SVD’s vasculature being underpopulated due to its lower trajectory count, though without ground truth we cannot rule out that the discrepancy instead reflects a bias introduced by ZCA’s rescaling of coherent eigenspaces. Overall, ZCA populates this cortical region more fully than SVD, with equivalent or better reconstruction in highly dense vascular territories.

The same gain in trajectory density and vascular completeness holds at the scale of the entire brain. Fig. 6 shows the complete reconstruction over 36 minutes of continuous acquisition, including the cortical region highlighted in Fig. 5 above: ZCA compensates for attenuation, more completely reconstructing vasculature at the bottom of the cortex and subcortex, with clearer patterns in high-density zoom regions (a-d) and fuller vasculature elsewhere (e-h). ZCA also suppresses skull clutter, seen as reduced tracking artifacts above the cortical surface, and enhances the large feeding and draining arteries and veins at the bottom of the brain (f-g), which are normally thinned by aliasing in SVD-filtered data. IV-D Spatial covariance AER enables longer ensembles to recover slow flow and capillary tracks Results up until now have focused on vessel reconstruction quality, but capillary-level flow is not resolved in Fig. 6 : forming the N t × N t N_{t}\times N_{t} temporal covariance matrix over long ensembles is memory-limited at the beamforming density used here (four points per wavelength), which was retained for image quality rather than reduced to permit longer ensembles. Increasing the temporal statistics inside the matrix decomposition resolves these stationary microbubbles, revealing blood transit through the entire arteriovenous tree [ 8 ] . Operating on the spatial rather than temporal covariance keeps this tractable over arbitrarily long ensembles without growing the covariance matrix size. Here we explore a 64 × 192 64\times 192 subcortical ROI; because this analysis uses a different covariance formulation and a much smaller field of view than Fig. 6 , the following figures use different intensity and velocity colormaps than the whole-brain visualization above. To estimate the optimal ensemble size, we measured the effective rank of the SVD decomposition as a function of temporal samples (Section III-D ); Fig.

7 (top left) shows it increasing sharply before plateauing at 15 s, the ensemble length used for the remainder of this section. The additional temporal statistics reveal, in both the filtered and tracking data, stationary bubbles in areas of dense microvasculature that remain separable from faster-moving scatterers, along with the arteriole-to-capillary-to-venule trajectories underlying the Single Capillary Reporter (SCaRe) metric (Section III-E ) [ 8 ] . Using SCaRe, we measured the number of full capillary tracks recovered by ZCA- and SVD-filtered data as a function of λ \lambda , mirroring the stable behavior seen in Fig. 3 : a high-pass filter initially increases capillary counts as stationary clutter is removed, then reduces them as spatiotemporal artifacts appear; the count per area per second remains stable across λ \lambda from 1 to 80, with ZCA and SVD converging to nearly the same value, though ZCA consistently records slightly more trajectories. Comparing density, velocity, and SCaRe-derived distributions for the same subcortical dataset (Fig. 8 ), density reconstructions show comparable resolution (FRC: 17.7 μ \mu m SVD, 18.1 μ \mu m ZCA), while ZCA’s velocity distribution extends further into the low-velocity range and yields longer capillary dwell times and a higher rate of fully connected capillary tracks: 1 capillary/s for SVD versus 5/s for ZCA (max 20/s), with the reconstructed capillary population correlating with low-velocity regions on the projected velocity maps. V Discussion Here we present adaptive eigenspectrum remapping (AER), instantiated as spatiotemporal ZCA whitening, as an alternative to SVD-based clutter filters for transcranial brain imaging and ULM. By removing correlations between spatiotemporal eigenspaces, AER with ZCA weighting enhances microbubble reconstruction and improves skull clutter suppression at large ensemble sizes.

Its most significant advantage is eliminating the manually tunable eigenvalue cutoff, which is still frequently implemented by hand despite proposed automated methods [ 11 ] , since the SVD is data-dependent and different acquisition configurations or anatomical targets require different cutoffs. Rather than selecting one, AER balances the spatiotemporal eigenspaces, rescaling highly coherent signals such as skull tissue toward the noise floor, generalizing the spectral flattening of the Wiener-Khinchin theorem [ 18 ] to the spatiotemporal domain while retaining the full signal. Because no data are discarded, reconstruction quality remains consistent across ensemble lengths and ZCA avoids SVD-related artifacts such as aliasing of high-velocity flow; unlike PCA whitening, it also preserves the original data space through back-projection, retaining information about flow directions. AER can be implemented before or after beamforming, on spatial or temporal covariance matrices, whichever is more convenient, and is broadly applicable wherever spatiotemporal data contain distinct flow regimes, particularly as gapless acquisition makes long temporal sequences increasingly practical. We framed this work under the broader AER term because whitening is only one choice of eigenvalue weights. Complete whitening flattens the spectrum to the noise floor, which our λ \lambda sweep shows suppresses clutter but also adds noise texture at heavy regularization. Other weightings may be preferable in some settings, for example partial whitening that compresses rather than flattens the clutter eigenvalues, shrinkage-type weights that leave the noise floor unamplified, or weights informed by the temporal frequency content of each eigenvector to emphasize slow or fast flow regimes selectively. Because these all share the same eigendecomposition and back-projection (Equation 9 ), they can be compared within one framework at no additional computational cost.

We leave the systematic comparison of AER weightings to future work. Several limitations remain: given the diversity of ultrasound applications, it remains to be established whether AER performs reliably under all conditions, and in microvascular regimes with significant tissue motion, such as myocardial imaging, estimating the eigenvector subspaces becomes more challenging, though we expect dominant coherent structures can still be identified with sufficient temporal sampling. Numerical precision is a further consideration, since the ZCA weighting’s inverse square root amplifies estimation error and floating-point round-off for small eigenvalues; Tikhonov regularization limits this by replacing λ k − 1 / 2 \lambda_{k}^{-1/2} with ( λ k + λ ) − 1 / 2 (\lambda_{k}+\lambda)^{-1/2} , at the cost of a controlled deviation from exact whitening, and the regularization level should be reported since it governs the balance between clutter suppression, flow preservation, and noise amplification. A separate consideration is the choice of decomposition: preliminary analysis suggests randomized SVD still requires accurate estimation of the full eigenvalue spectrum, making full subspace estimation preferable for AER. Future work should investigate whether a single transformation matrix W W can be estimated a priori for an entire dataset and applied in real time. VI Conclusions In this work, we introduced adaptive eigenspectrum remapping (AER) and investigated ZCA matrix whitening as an AER weighting and an alternative to hard-thresholded SVD clutter filtering for transcranial microbubble imaging and ULM in the mouse brain. By rescaling the covariance eigenspectrum rather than discarding selected modes, ZCA reduces the dominance of highly coherent clutter while retaining weak and slow-flow components.

Across temporal and spatial covariance formulations, ZCA improved microbubble contrast and vascular image quality, produced higher trajectory density, and revealed more low-velocity flow in ULM reconstructions. With sufficiently long temporal ensembles, spatial AER maintained stable reconstructions, while SCaRe analysis showed more complete capillary networks and connected artery-to-capillary-to-vein trajectories than SVD. These results support AER as a flexible, data-adaptive alternative to manually selected SVD cutoffs, although its performance remains dependent on covariance estimation, numerical precision, and the choice of regularization. More broadly, the results suggest that remapping the covariance eigenspectrum, of which whitening is one instance, can improve microvascular reconstruction while preserving information that threshold-based clutter filtering may remove.
